sections.heading: What is Python?
content: Python is an easy-to-read, high-level programming language created by Guido van Rossum, first released in 1991. It was designed so that code reads almost like plain English.
That readability makes Python great for beginners, but it also powers production systems at companies like Google, Netflix, Instagram, and NASA.

It's used worldwide across many domains: **Web Development** (Django, FastAPI, Flask), **Data Science** (Pandas, NumPy), **AI & Machine Learning** (PyTorch, TensorFlow), **Automation & Scripting**, and **Cybersecurity** (writing tools, analyzing malware, penetration testing).
Python is an **interpreted language** the interpreter reads and runs your code line by line, rather than compiling it all upfront. That makes testing and debugging fast.
In Python, we use the **print()** function to display text or numbers on the screen. This is called **output** how your program communicates results back to the user.

Example: `print("Hello, World!")` displays `Hello, World!` in the terminal. `print` is a **built-in function**, and whatever sits inside the parentheses `()` is called an **argument** the data being sent to the function to display.

sections.heading: Setting Up Your Python Environment
content: Before you can run any Python code, you need Python installed on your machine along with a place to write your code this is what Exercise 1 ("Setting Up") is all about.

**Current version:** as of August 2026, the latest stable release is **Python 3.14.7** (released Aug 5, 2026), with **Python 3.13.15** still actively maintained as the previous stable line. **Python 3.15** is in release-candidate stage and scheduled for full release around October 2026 not recommended for beginners yet.

**Step 1 — Download:** go to the official source, **python.org/downloads**. It auto-detects your OS and recommends the right installer. Never download Python from third-party sites official installers only, to avoid malware or tampered builds.

**Step 2 — Install (Windows):** run the installer and make sure to check **'Add Python to PATH'** before clicking Install. This lets you type `python` directly in Command Prompt or PowerShell. Windows users can also use the newer **Python Install Manager (MSIX)**, or install via `winget install Python.Python.3.14`.
**Step 2 — Install (Mac):** the official installer from python.org works well, or use Homebrew: `brew install python`.
**Step 2 — Install (Linux):** most distros ship with Python pre-installed. Check with `python3 --version`; if missing, install via your package manager, e.g. `sudo apt install python3`.

**Step 3 — Verify installation:** open your terminal and type `python --version` (or `python3 --version` on Mac/Linux). You should see something like `Python 3.14.7`. This confirms Python is correctly installed and accessible.

**Step 4 — Choose an editor:** you'll need somewhere to write code. Python ships with a basic editor called **IDLE**, but most learners use **VS Code** (free, lightweight, huge extension ecosystem) with the official Python extension installed.
**Step 5 — Run your first file:** save a file as `hello.py`, then run it from the terminal with `python hello.py`. If it prints your message, your setup is complete and you're ready for Exercise 2.

sections.heading: Syntax & Formatting
content: **Syntax** is the set of rules that define how Python code must be written for the interpreter to understand it. Getting it wrong raises a `SyntaxError`.

Text strings in Python must be enclosed inside single (`'...'`) or double (`"..."`) quotes. Both work identically `print('Hi')` and `print("Hi")` give the same output. Use double quotes when your text itself contains an apostrophe, e.g. `"It's sunny today"`.

Any quoted text is called a **string** a core Python data type representing words, sentences, or any sequence of characters. You'll use strings heavily in the upcoming **Pattern**, **Initials**, and **Snail Mail** exercises, where you'll print names, shapes, and addresses.
Lines starting with **#** are comments, ignored by the execution engine. They're notes for humans useful for explaining code, leaving reminders, or disabling a line temporarily without deleting it.
Example: `# This line prints a greeting` followed by `print("Hello!")` only the `print()` line actually runs; the comment is skipped entirely.
Python is **case-sensitive** and uses **indentation** (spacing) instead of curly braces `{}` to define blocks of code you'll meet this properly once loops and conditionals show up in later stations.
Each statement usually sits on its own line, and unlike Java or C++, Python doesn't require a semicolon `;` at the end of a line.
